items_missed: THE VIRTUAL WALKTHROUGH WAS NEVER SCHEDULED. This is the defining miss of the call and the reason it classifies as a walkthrough scheduler. He raised it twice — 'one thing that we do, we get a virtual walkthrough just because I don't want to set it up two trucks. You need a third truck' and again at the close, 'in the estimate that I sent over again we still need to do a virtual, I want to take a look at everything for you' — and never proposed a day, never proposed a time, never sent a link, and never asked the customer when he was free. On a 5,300 sq ft job where he himself cannot resolve three trucks versus four, the walkthrough is the entire product of this call and it does not exist.

Customer's name was not captured until minute fifteen, after the full quote had already been delivered, and only because the customer asked for the estimate in writing. Twenty-one minutes of work on a $14,000 opportunity ran anonymously.
No agenda statement, no 'sound good?', and no availability check. Never once said Einstein has October 7-10 open, on a customer working against a hard closing date.

No quote form recap. At minute fifteen he asked 'I think he might have done an online inquiry already. Did you?' and the customer said yes — then Joel moved on without pulling it, so nothing on file was reconciled against anything he had just quoted.

Packing needs never asked. Not once, in twenty-one minutes, on a 5,300 sq ft five-bedroom two-story home moving 250 miles in three days. On a home that size a full or partial pack is potentially several thousand dollars and multiple additional days, and it was never raised. This is the largest revenue miss on the board.
Box count never asked, for the same reason.

Special considerations and walk distance never asked, on eight acres with a separate barn. The distance from the barn to where a 26-foot truck can actually park is a first-order driver of the load hours he was estimating, and it was never established.

Access concerns — driveway, gate, turning radius for three or four 26-footers on an eight-acre property — never asked at the origin, and nothing at all was asked about the destination, which he does not have an address for.
Destination floors never asked. He got 'Two story' for the origin at minute fifteen and never asked anything about the unload property.

Moving stressors never asked. The customer spent five minutes working a genuine problem out loud — 'we have to have everything out and the house cleaned by the morning of October 9th' — and Joel engaged it purely as truck logistics. No acknowledgment that a closing-day squeeze with a buyer negotiation attached is stressful, no 'what's worrying you most about this.'

What's included was never stated. No gas, truck, taxes, tools, bands or pads as included value — the ninety blankets per truck were mentioned as an operational practice, not as something the customer is getting for free.

Disassembly and reassembly were never stated as included. The only mention ran the other way: 'we can move this on just as long as this disassembled already, we don't necessarily have like the expertise or like our guys aren't used to disassembling on those.'
Meet Your Mover and the On-Time Guarantee were both never mentioned.

No 'no hidden fees' pitch, on the call in this batch with the most fees. $240 per truck overnight, $1,056 per truck travel, $115 per truck return — stacked three deep with no framing, which is what produced 'Man, that seems that, that's pretty expensive you all.'

Fifteen-minute proration never mentioned. The customer is being quoted roughly $14,500 on an hourly basis with two padded day estimates and was never told he only pays for time actually used to the nearest quarter hour. That single sentence is the direct answer to 'that seems high' and it was never said.

No typical time range given for a home this size. He gave a resource benchmark — 'typically for a 4000 square foot home plus we typically need four trucks' — but never an hours benchmark the customer could test the seven-hour and ten-hour day assumptions against.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10, on the call where it was worth the most money in the batch. At six movers and $95 to $102 per mover per hour, an hour of prep saves roughly $600. The customer twice offered to move things himself ('I'll just, I'll have my own truck or trailer' and 'maybe I'll move that myself. I can have like if you all load in my bed in my truck') and Joel pushed back on liability grounds both times without ever redirecting to the version that carries no liability question — small, loose, personal items in the customer's own vehicle. He talked a motivated customer out of the one behavior that would have lowered his own bill.

SpareFoot referral never made, on the one call where it was the actual solution. The customer needed an overnight hold between closing dates, Joel said 'We'd have to like pop it off at a storage unit,' and then produced no storage option, no partner, no referral, and no path — leaving the whole timing problem unsolved.

Zero booking attempt and zero date hold. The customer named the window himself ('we're looking at October 7th... we close on the ninth'), and Joel never offered to soft-hold anything on a date he had not even confirmed was available.

No deposit required was never mentioned. A customer who has just said 'that seems pretty expensive' and asked for a military discount is a customer who needs to hear that holding the date costs nothing and no money changes hands until the move is done. It never came.

No bolded-details framing and no 'reply with any corrections' on the email — which matters unusually much here, because the emailed breakdown is the only artifact of a twenty-one-minute call and the customer is taking it to his wife as the sole record.
Customer's name never used once. He got 'Justin Bradshaw' at minute fifteen and did not speak it again.

Customer's mood declined over the call rather than improving. 'Man, that seems that, that's pretty expensive you all,' then 'That doesn't make sense' at the $2,000 coverage cap, then 'No, I just wanna see it on paper so I can show my wife' — a polite disengagement, not a warm close.
top_strength: The insurance conversation is genuinely the best piece of consultative honesty on this board, and Joel handled it under pressure. When the customer said his dining set alone cost $15,000 and asked 'you only do $2,000 like per item or total?', Joel gave the answer that hurts — 'Total per move' — without softening it, and then immediately did the right thing for the customer rather than for the sale: 'I would probably get a third party insurance for some of these items. You can look at a company called bakers insurance if you'd like and they can kind of ensure and make sure that you're all good there.' When the customer pushed back that the cap is inadequate, Joel did not get defensive; he reframed against the real industry benchmark with a worked example: 'most moving companies not sure if you're aware but they offer 60¢ per pound. So, let's just say, if they damage your TV or, or even let's say your table £400 they'll end up paying like $253 to settle that... again 60¢ per pound we do way better than just the industry standard.' That is the rubric's insurance bullet delivered properly, and he delivered it to a skeptical customer on a $15,000 item. He also probed specialty items well and got a material answer — 'do you have anything like large that's made at a glass, marble stone' produced the 400-pound table, the gym equipment and the sauna, all of which change the crew plan. His fee explanations were specific and correctly decomposed rather than lumped ($1,056 per truck travel, $240 per truck overnight, $115 per truck return from Celina), and his arithmetic across two days actually checks out to the $14,000-$15,000 he quoted. And on the closing-date problem he showed real operational judgment, explaining the risk in terms of the customer's exposure rather than Einstein's convenience, and closing with the only proper sense-check on the call: 'let's just say worst case scenario you don't end up closing on the house that day then we just have your stuff whole held and then we can't utilize the truck that day. Does that make sense?'
coaching_note: Rubric fit caveat: this classifies as a walkthrough scheduler — 5,300 sq ft, and Joel explicitly routed to a virtual walkthrough — so the pricing, clock, estimate and Save Your Ass sections do not cleanly apply and the 32 should be read as directional rather than comparable to a straight intake call. That said, the walkthrough-scheduler read makes the result worse, not better, because the one thing this call had to produce is the one thing it did not: the walkthrough was raised twice and never scheduled. There is no date, no time, no link, no next step. Fix that first and fix it as a hard rule — on any job that routes to a walkthrough, the walkthrough gets a calendar slot before the call ends, and nothing else on the call matters as much. Second priority, and it is a large one: he quoted a 5,300 sq ft five-bedroom home and never asked whether they need packing. That is not a rubric technicality — on a home this size it is potentially several thousand dollars of service and an extra day of crew time, and its absence also means the day-one seven-hour load estimate is built on an assumption nobody verified. Third, estimate-accuracy flag, and this is the strongest one in the batch. Joel used the word 'conservative' twice in the same quote — 'let's just say conservative, a conservative estimate' on day one, and 'I'm estimating like a six hour unload just kind of being a little conservative there' on day two — while simultaneously telling the customer he did not trust his own truck count: 'I'll be completely honest with you typically for a 4000 square foot home plus we typically need four trucks,' then quoting three. Padding both days and then pricing per truck on a truck count he distrusts is how a $14,000 number becomes a $15,000 number for no reason the customer can see, and it is exactly the conservative-on-large-homes pattern the estimate-accuracy rock is chasing. The customer's response was the predictable one: 'Man, that seems that, that's pretty expensive you all.' The right sequencing is the opposite — do not quote at all until the walkthrough resolves the truck count, and if a directional number is needed, give a range with the driver named: 'the honest answer is it's three trucks or four and that swings this by about $3,000, which is exactly why I want twenty minutes on video before I put a number in front of your wife.' Fourth: the fee stack was never defended with the mechanism that defends it. He never said fifteen-minute proration, never said no deposit, and never said no hidden fees — three sentences that together answer 'that seems high' far better than anything he actually said. Fifth: he had a customer who volunteered twice to move things himself and he talked him out of it. The liability concern about loading a customer's rented trailer is legitimate; the response should have redirected rather than closed the door — 'I'd rather not load your trailer for liability reasons, but everything small and loose you can carload yourself, absolutely do it. At six guys on the clock every hour you save us is real money.' Finally, twenty-one minutes is too long for what this call produced. He re-asked how the customer heard about Einstein twice, circled the closing-date logistics four separate times without resolving it, narrated his own calculator work repeatedly, and spent a stretch disparaging larger carriers ('he contracts workers off of Craig's list') that landed flat — 'Yeah. We've never done that.' That time belonged to packing, access, walk distance, and booking the walkthrough.
phone_presence_notes: Twenty-one minutes with the customer's name never spoken once, long stretches of audible calculator work ('Give me one second here,' 'Okay, let's see here,' 'The seven hours.' 'Five.'), and every emotional cue left unhandled — the closing-date squeeze was treated purely as truck logistics, 'that seems pretty expensive' drew a flat no-discount answer with no reframe, and 'That doesn't make sense' on the coverage cap got 'Yup, but, but I'll' before he moved on.

We've never done that' suggests the latter but is not conclusive.
